note.text:
To multiply AB, multiply each row of A by each column of B: multiply the pairs of elements and add.
• Row 1 of A × column 1 of B gives the element in row 1, column 1 of AB, and so on.
• AB exists only if the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. An m × n matrix times an n × p matrix gives an m × p matrix.
• In general AB ≠ BA: the order of multiplication matters.
• The identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged: AI = IA = A.

sections.heading: Row times column
sections.text:
Matrix multiplication is not done element by element. Each element of AB comes from a row of A and a column of B:
multiply the first elements, multiply the second elements, and add.
For A = {matStr([[2, 1], [3, 4]])} and B = {matStr([[1, 5], [2, 0]])}: row {1} of A is ({2}, {1}) and column {1} of B is ({1}, {2}), so the top-left element of AB is {2} × {1} + {1} × {2} = {4}.

sections.heading: When can we multiply?
sections.text:
Each row of A must have as many elements as each column of B. So the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B.
Write the orders side by side: ({2} × {3})({3} × {1}). The inside numbers match ({3} and {3}), so AB exists, and its order is the outside numbers: {2} × {1}.
If the inside numbers differ, AB cannot be found.

sections.heading: Order matters
sections.text:
With numbers, {3} × {5} = {5} × {3}. With matrices, AB and BA are usually different, and one of them may not even exist.
The identity matrix I = {matStr([[1, 0], [0, 1]])} is special: AI = IA = A for any {2} × {2} matrix A.
A² means A × A, row times column, not each element squared.
